title: Trigonometry
description: Radian measure, unit circle, exact values, Pythagorean identity, trig graphs and transformations, solving equations, sine rule, cosine rule, area of triangle, and double angle formulas.

notes.heading: Radian Measure and the Unit Circle
notes.body:
Radians give a natural way to measure angles by relating them directly to arc length. One full revolution is $360^{\circ}$ or $2\pi$ radians.

📌 Definition
A radian is the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius.
    $$2\pi 	ext{ rad} = 360^{\circ}$$
    $$\pi 	ext{ rad} = 180^{\circ}$$

🔑 Converting Between Degrees and Radians
    To radians:   multiply by $\dfrac{\pi}{180}$
    To degrees:   multiply by $\dfrac{180}{\pi}$

💡 Worked Example — Converting Angles
Convert $150^{\circ}$ to radians and $\dfrac{5\pi}{4}$ rad to degrees.

  Step 1: Degrees to radians
    $$150^{\circ} 	imes \dfrac{\pi}{180} = \dfrac{5\pi}{6} 	ext{ rad}$$

  Step 2: Radians to degrees
    $$\dfrac{5\pi}{4} 	imes \dfrac{180}{\pi} = 225^{\circ}$$

📎 Common Exact Values
• $30^{\circ} = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$
• $45^{\circ} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$
• $60^{\circ} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$
• $90^{\circ} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$
• $180^{\circ} = \pi$
• $270^{\circ} = \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$

🔑 Arc Length and Sector Area
For a circle of radius $r$ and central angle $	heta$ (in radians):
    Arc length:     $l = r	heta$
    Sector area:    $A = \dfrac{1}{2} r^2 	heta$

💡 Worked Example — Sector Calculations
A sector has radius $6$ cm and central angle $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ rad. Find the arc length and sector area.

  Step 1: Arc length
    $l = 6 	imes \dfrac{\pi}{3} = 2\pi$ cm $\approx 6.28$ cm

  Step 2: Sector area
    $A = \dfrac{1}{2} 	imes 6^2 	imes \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{1}{2} 	imes 36 	imes \dfrac{\pi}{3} = 6\pi$ cm$^2$ $\approx 18.85$ cm$^2$

🔑 The Unit Circle
On a unit circle (radius = 1), any angle $	heta$ measured anticlockwise from the positive x-axis has terminal point:
    $$(\cos 	heta, \sin 	heta)$$

This definition works for ALL angles, not just acute ones.

📊 CAST Rule — Signs in Each Quadrant
• Quadrant 1 ($0^{\circ}$ to $90^{\circ}$):   All positive
• Quadrant 2 ($90^{\circ}$ to $180^{\circ}$):  Sine positive
• Quadrant 3 ($180^{\circ}$ to $270^{\circ}$): Tangent positive
• Quadrant 4 ($270^{\circ}$ to $360^{\circ}$): Cosine positive

A helpful mnemonic: "All Students Take Calculus"

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting to check the quadrant when finding $\sin$ or $\cos$ from a known ratio. If $\sin 	heta = \dfrac{1}{2}$, $	heta$ could be $30^{\circ}$ (Q1) OR $150^{\circ}$ (Q2). Always draw a quick sketch.

illustration.alt: The unit circle showing (cosθ, sinθ) coordinates; key trig identities including sin²θ+cos²θ=1 and double-angle formulas; sine and cosine rules for non-right triangles; and trig graphs with amplitude and period.
illustration.caption: Trigonometry extends beyond right triangles with the unit circle. Key identities let you simplify expressions and solve equations. The sine and cosine rules handle any triangle.

notes.heading: Identities and Solving Equations
notes.body:
Trigonometric identities let you rewrite expressions and solve equations. The Pythagorean identity is the most important — it connects sine and cosine.

📌 Definition
An identity is an equation that is true for ALL values of the variable (where both sides are defined).

🔑 Pythagorean Identity
    $$\sin^2 	heta + \cos^2 	heta = 1$$

Rearranged forms (useful for solving):
    $$\sin^2 	heta = 1 - \cos^2 	heta$$
    $$\cos^2 	heta = 1 - \sin^2 	heta$$

💡 Worked Example — Using the Identity
Given $\cos 	heta = \dfrac{3}{5}$ and $	heta$ is in Q1, find $\sin 	heta$.

  Step 1: Substitute into the identity
    $$\sin^2 	heta + \left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)^2 = 1$$
    $$\sin^2 	heta + \dfrac{9}{25} = 1$$

  Step 2: Solve for $\sin^2 	heta$
    $$\sin^2 	heta = \dfrac{16}{25}$$

  Step 3: Take the square root
    $$\sin 	heta = \dfrac{4}{5}$$  (positive because $	heta$ is in Q1)

🔑 Double Angle Formulas
    $$\sin 2	heta = 2 \sin 	heta \cos 	heta$$
    $$\cos 2	heta = \cos^2 	heta - \sin^2 	heta = 2\cos^2 	heta - 1 = 1 - 2\sin^2 	heta$$
    $$	an 2	heta = \dfrac{2 	an 	heta}{1 - 	an^2 	heta}$$

💡 Worked Example — Double Angle
If $\sin 	heta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$ and $\cos 	heta = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}$, find $\cos 2	heta$.

  Step 1: Choose the most convenient form
    $$\cos 2	heta = \cos^2 	heta - \sin^2 	heta$$

  Step 2: Substitute values
    $$\cos 2	heta = \left(\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\right)^2 - \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\right)^2$$
    $$\cos 2	heta = \dfrac{4}{5} - \dfrac{1}{5} = \dfrac{3}{5}$$

🔑 Solving Trigonometric Equations — Step-by-Step
1. Isolate the trig ratio ($\sin$, $\cos$, or $	an$) if possible
2. Find the principal value using inverse trig on your calculator
3. Use symmetry and periodicity to find ALL solutions in the given interval
4. For quadratics in $\sin$ or $\cos$, substitute $u = \sin 	heta$ or $u = \cos 	heta$, then factorise

💡 Worked Example — Solving a Quadratic Trig Equation
Solve $2\cos^2 	heta - \cos 	heta - 1 = 0$ for $0^{\circ} \leq 	heta \leq 360^{\circ}$.

  Step 1: Substitute $u = \cos 	heta$
    $$2u^2 - u - 1 = 0$$

  Step 2: Factorise
    $$(2u + 1)(u - 1) = 0$$

  Step 3: Solve for $u$
    $$u = 1 \quad 	ext{or} \quad u = -\dfrac{1}{2}$$
    $$\cos 	heta = 1 \quad 	ext{or} \quad \cos 	heta = -\dfrac{1}{2}$$

  Step 4: Find all angles in $[0^{\circ}, 360^{\circ}]$
    $$\cos 	heta = 1 \rightarrow 	heta = 0^{\circ}$$
    $$\cos 	heta = -\dfrac{1}{2} \rightarrow 	heta = 120^{\circ}, 240^{\circ}$$

  Answer: $$	heta = 0^{\circ}, 120^{\circ}, 240^{\circ}$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Always state the domain before solving
• Sine and cosine repeat every $360^{\circ}$ (or $2\pi$ rad)
• Tangent repeats every $180^{\circ}$ (or $\pi$ rad)
• Check your final answers by substituting back into the original equation

⚠️ Common Mistake
Dividing both sides of an equation by $\sin 	heta$ or $\cos 	heta$ — this loses solutions where that term equals zero. Always factorise instead of dividing.

notes.heading: Graphs of Trigonometric Functions
notes.body:
Trigonometric functions are periodic — their graphs repeat forever. Understanding how the parameters transform the basic graphs is essential for modelling real-world cycles.

📌 Definition
A periodic function repeats its values at regular intervals. The shortest such interval is called the period.

🔑 General Form of Sinusoidal Functions
    $$y = a \sin(b(x - c)) + d$$
    $$y = a \cos(b(x - c)) + d$$

Parameter meanings:
• $a$ = amplitude (vertical stretch; $|a|$ is the height from midline to peak)
• $b$ = affects the period; period = $\dfrac{2\pi}{|b|}$ for $\sin$/$\cos$, or $\dfrac{\pi}{|b|}$ for $	an$
• $c$ = phase shift (horizontal translation)
• $d$ = vertical shift (moves the principal axis up or down)

💡 Worked Example — Finding Amplitude and Period
For $y = 4 \sin(3x) - 2$, state the amplitude and period.

  Step 1: Identify $a$ and $b$
    $a = 4$,  $b = 3$

  Step 2: Calculate amplitude
    Amplitude = $|a| = 4$

  Step 3: Calculate period
    Period = $\dfrac{2\pi}{|b|} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$

  Step 4: Note the vertical shift
    Principal axis is $y = -2$ (so the graph oscillates between $y = 2$ and $y = -6$)

📊 Key Features of Basic Graphs

$y = \sin x$:
• Passes through $(0, 0)$
• Maximum at $(\dfrac{\pi}{2}, 1)$
• Zero at $(\pi, 0)$
• Minimum at $(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}, -1)$
• Period: $2\pi$

$y = \cos x$:
• Starts at $(0, 1)$
• Zero at $(\dfrac{\pi}{2}, 0)$
• Minimum at $(\pi, -1)$
• Period: $2\pi$

$y = 	an x$:
• Zero at $(0, 0)$, $(\pi, 0)$, etc.
• Vertical asymptotes at $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} + n\pi$
• Period: $\pi$

💡 Worked Example — Describing a Transformed Graph
Describe the transformation from $y = \cos x$ to $y = -20 \cos(3x)$.

  Step 1: Amplitude
    $|-20| = 20$. The amplitude is $20$.

  Step 2: Period
    Period = $\dfrac{360^{\circ}}{3} = 120^{\circ}$ (or $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ rad)

  Step 3: Reflection
    The negative sign reflects the graph in the x-axis.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Amplitude is always positive — take the absolute value of $a$
• Phase shift is $c$ units to the RIGHT (note the minus sign inside the bracket)
• For tan graphs, there are no maxima or minima — the curve extends to $\pm \infty$

⚠️ Common Mistake
Confusing period with frequency. A larger value of $b$ makes the graph MORE squashed horizontally (shorter period), not stretched. If $b = 2$, the period is halved.

notes.heading: Sine Rule, Cosine Rule, and Triangle Area
notes.body:
For non-right-angled triangles, we need three powerful tools: the sine rule, the cosine rule, and the area formula using sine. Each is suited to different given information.

📌 Notation
For triangle ABC:
• Side $a$ is opposite angle $A$
• Side $b$ is opposite angle $B$
• Side $c$ is opposite angle $C$

🔑 The Sine Rule
    $$\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B} = \dfrac{c}{\sin C}$$

Or equivalently:
    $$\dfrac{\sin A}{a} = \dfrac{\sin B}{b} = \dfrac{\sin C}{c}$$

Use the sine rule when you know:
• Two angles and one side (AAS or ASA)
• Two sides and a non-included angle (SSA — but watch for the ambiguous case)

💡 Worked Example — Sine Rule (AAS)
In triangle ABC, angle $A = 40^{\circ}$, angle $B = 70^{\circ}$, and side $a = 8$ cm. Find side $b$.

  Step 1: Set up the sine rule
    $$\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B}$$

  Step 2: Substitute known values
    $$\dfrac{8}{\sin 40^{\circ}} = \dfrac{b}{\sin 70^{\circ}}$$

  Step 3: Solve for $b$
    $$b = \dfrac{8 \sin 70^{\circ}}{\sin 40^{\circ}}$$
    $b \approx 11.7$ cm (3 sf)

🔑 The Cosine Rule
    $$a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc \cos A$$

To find an angle when all three sides are known:
    $$\cos A = \dfrac{b^2 + c^2 - a^2}{2bc}$$

Use the cosine rule when you know:
• Two sides and the included angle (SAS)
• All three sides (SSS)

💡 Worked Example — Cosine Rule (SAS)
Find side $a$ when $b = 5$ cm, $c = 7$ cm, and angle $A = 60^{\circ}$.

  Step 1: Apply the cosine rule
    $$a^2 = 5^2 + 7^2 - 2 	imes 5 	imes 7 	imes \cos 60^{\circ}$$

  Step 2: Calculate
    $$a^2 = 25 + 49 - 70 	imes 0.5$$
    $$a^2 = 74 - 35 = 39$$

  Step 3: Solve
    $a = \sqrt{39} \approx 6.24$ cm (3 sf)

🔑 Area of a Triangle
    $$	ext{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} ab \sin C$$

Use this when you know two sides and the included angle.

💡 Worked Example — Area Formula
A triangle has sides $9$ cm and $12$ cm with an included angle of $45^{\circ}$. Find its area.

  Step 1: Substitute into the formula
    $$	ext{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} 	imes 9 	imes 12 	imes \sin 45^{\circ}$$

  Step 2: Evaluate
    $$	ext{Area} = 54 	imes \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = 27\sqrt{2} 	ext{ cm}^2 \approx 38.2 	ext{ cm}^2$$

📎 When to Use Each Rule
• Sine rule: AAS, ASA, SSA (with caution)
• Cosine rule: SAS, SSS
• Area formula: two sides and included angle

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using the cosine rule with the wrong angle. The angle in $\cos A$ must be the included angle between sides $b$ and $c$. If you are finding angle $A$, make sure side $a$ is opposite it.

notes.heading: The Ambiguous Case of the Sine Rule
notes.body:
When you are given two sides and a non-included acute angle (SSA), the sine rule can sometimes produce TWO valid triangles. This is called the ambiguous case.

📌 Definition
The ambiguous case occurs when using the sine rule with SSA data, specifically when the side opposite the given angle is SHORTER than the other known side but LONGER than the altitude from the other known side.

🔑 The Three Possibilities
Given angle $A$ (acute), side $a$ (opposite $A$), and side $b$ (adjacent to $A$):

    Calculate the altitude:  $h = b \sin A$

Then compare $a$ with $h$ and $b$:

1. If $a < h$ → no triangle is possible
2. If $a = h$ → exactly one right-angled triangle
3. If $h < a < b$ → TWO triangles are possible
4. If $a \geq b$ → exactly one triangle

💡 Worked Example — The Ambiguous Case
In triangle ABC, $a = 8$, $b = 12$, and angle $A = 35^{\circ}$. Determine how many triangles can be formed.

  Step 1: Calculate the altitude
    $h = b \sin A = 12 	imes \sin 35^{\circ} \approx 6.88$

  Step 2: Compare $a$ with $h$ and $b$
    $h \approx 6.88 < a = 8 < b = 12$

  Step 3: Conclusion
    Since $h < a < b$, TWO triangles are possible.

  Step 4: Find both solutions (optional working)
    Using $\sin B = \dfrac{b \sin A}{a} = \dfrac{12 \sin 35^{\circ}}{8} \approx 0.860$

    Solution 1: $B \approx 59.4^{\circ}$ (acute)
    Solution 2: $B \approx 180^{\circ} - 59.4^{\circ} = 120.6^{\circ}$ (obtuse)

    Both give valid triangles because $A + B < 180^{\circ}$ in each case.

🔑 Why Two Solutions Exist
The sine function is positive in both Quadrant 1 and Quadrant 2. So if $\sin B = k$ (where $0 < k < 1$), there are two possible angles:
    $$B = \sin^{-1}(k) \quad 	ext{(acute)}$$
    $$B = 180^{\circ} - \sin^{-1}(k) \quad 	ext{(obtuse)}$$

Both may give valid triangles if the angle sum does not exceed $180^{\circ}$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The ambiguous case ONLY happens with SSA and an acute given angle
• If the given angle is obtuse or right, there is at most one triangle
• Always check whether $A + B < 180^{\circ}$ for each possible value of $B$

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting to check the second (obtuse) solution. When you use $\sin^{-1}$ on your calculator, it always gives the acute angle. You must also consider $180^{\circ}$ minus that value.

notes.heading: Compound Angle Identities
notes.body:
Compound angle identities let you expand expressions like $\sin(A+B)$ and $\cos(A-B)$. They are essential for rewriting trig expressions and solving equations that cannot be simplified with the Pythagorean identity alone.

📌 Definition
For all angles $A$ and $B$:
    $$\sin(A+B) = \sin A \cos B + \cos A \sin B$$
    $$\sin(A-B) = \sin A \cos B - \cos A \sin B$$
    $$\cos(A+B) = \cos A \cos B - \sin A \sin B$$
    $$\cos(A-B) = \cos A \cos B + \sin A \sin B$$

🔑 Key Concept
These formulas replace a single trig ratio of a combined angle with products of ratios of the separate angles. The sign pattern matters: $\sin$ keeps the sign, while $\cos$ changes it.

💡 Worked Example — Expanding $\sin 75^{\circ}$
Find the exact value of $\sin 75^{\circ}$.

  Step 1: Split the angle
    $$\sin 75^{\circ} = \sin(45^{\circ} + 30^{\circ})$$

  Step 2: Apply the identity
    $$\sin(45^{\circ} + 30^{\circ}) = \sin 45^{\circ}\cos 30^{\circ} + \cos 45^{\circ}\sin 30^{\circ}$$

  Step 3: Substitute exact values
    $$= \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2}$$

  Step 4: Simplify
    $$= \dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{4} + \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{4} = \dfrac{\sqrt{6}+\sqrt{2}}{4}$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• $\sin(A+B) 
eq \sin A + \sin B$ — never distribute the function across the bracket.
• For $\cos(A+B)$ the middle sign is MINUS, and for $\cos(A-B)$ it is PLUS.
• These identities are valid for all real angles $A$ and $B$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting the sign swap in the cosine identities:
    $$\cos(A+B) = \cos A \cos B - \sin A \sin B$$
    $$\cos(A-B) = \cos A \cos B + \sin A \sin B$$
A plus inside the bracket becomes minus in the expansion, and vice versa.

✅ Check
Use the identities to show that $\cos 90^{\circ} = 0$:
    $$\cos(60^{\circ} + 30^{\circ}) = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = 0.$$

notes.heading: Inverse Trigonometric Functions
notes.body:
Inverse trig functions undo the action of sine, cosine, and tangent. Because trig functions are not one-to-one, their inverses are defined on restricted domains.

📌 Definition
The inverse trigonometric functions are:
    $$y = \sin^{-1} x \quad 	ext{(arcsin)}$$
    $$y = \cos^{-1} x \quad 	ext{(arccos)}$$
    $$y = 	an^{-1} x \quad 	ext{(arctan)}$$

Each gives the angle $y$ whose sine, cosine, or tangent is $x$.

🔑 Key Concept — Domains and Principal Ranges
For the inverse functions to be functions, the original trig function is restricted:

• $\sin^{-1} x$ has domain $[-1, 1]$ and range $[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}]$
• $\cos^{-1} x$ has domain $[-1, 1]$ and range $[0, \pi]$
• $	an^{-1} x$ has domain $\mathbb{R}$ and range $(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2})$

💡 Worked Example — Evaluating an Inverse
Find the exact value of $\cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$.

  Step 1: Set up the equation
    Let $y = \cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$, so $\cos y = -\dfrac{1}{2}$.

  Step 2: Use the principal range
    The range of $\cos^{-1}$ is $[0, \pi]$, where cosine is negative in Q2.

  Step 3: Solve
    $$y = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• $\sin^{-1} x$ does NOT mean $(\sin x)^{-1}$; the latter is the reciprocal $\csc x$.
• The output of an inverse trig function is always a single angle in the principal range.
• Inverse trig functions can be used to write the general solution of trig equations.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing $\sin^{-1}(\sin 210^{\circ}) = 210^{\circ}$. Because the principal range of $\sin^{-1}$ is $[-90^{\circ}, 90^{\circ}]$, the correct value is:
    $$\sin^{-1}(\sin 210^{\circ}) = -30^{\circ}$$

✅ Check
Evaluate $	an^{-1}(1)$.
    $	an^{-1}(1) = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$, since $	an \dfrac{\pi}{4} = 1$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ lies in $(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2})$.

notes.heading: Worked Examples: Advanced Trigonometry
notes.body:
The following worked examples bring together equations, identities, the sine and cosine rules in three dimensions, bearings, and periodic modelling. These are typical of harder DP-style questions.

💡 Worked Example — Trigonometric Equation with Identities
Solve $2\cos^2 x - \sin x - 1 = 0$ for $0 \leq x \leq 2\pi$.

  Step 1: Use the Pythagorean identity to write everything in terms of $\sin x$
    $$2(1 - \sin^2 x) - \sin x - 1 = 0$$

  Step 2: Simplify
    $$2 - 2\sin^2 x - \sin x - 1 = 0$$
    $$-2\sin^2 x - \sin x + 1 = 0$$
    $$2\sin^2 x + \sin x - 1 = 0$$

  Step 3: Factor
    $$(2\sin x - 1)(\sin x + 1) = 0$$

  Step 4: Solve
    $$\sin x = \dfrac{1}{2} \quad 	ext{or} \quad \sin x = -1$$

    $\sin x = \dfrac{1}{2}$ gives $x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$
    $\sin x = -1$ gives $x = \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$

  Solutions: $\boxed{x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{5\pi}{6}, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}}$

💡 Worked Example — Sine and Cosine Rules in 3D
A cuboid has base dimensions $6$ cm by $8$ cm and height $5$ cm. Point $P$ is on the top face directly above one corner, and point $Q$ is on the base diagonally opposite that corner. Find the angle between the line $PQ$ and the base.

  Step 1: Draw a diagram and label the base diagonal
    Base diagonal $d = \sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{100} = 10$ cm.

  Step 2: The vertical height is perpendicular to the base
    The line $PQ$, the base diagonal, and the vertical height form a right-angled triangle with vertical side $5$ cm and base side $10$ cm.

  Step 3: Find the angle with the base
    $$	an 	heta = \dfrac{5}{10} = \dfrac{1}{2}$$
    $$	heta = 	an^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \approx 26.6^{\circ}$$

💡 Worked Example — Bearings
A ship sails from port $A$ on bearing $060^{\circ}$ for $12$ km to point $B$. It then sails on bearing $150^{\circ}$ for $16$ km to point $C$. Find the bearing of $C$ from $A$.

  Step 1: Find the angle between the two legs at $B$
    Back bearing of $AB$ is $060^{\circ} + 180^{\circ} = 240^{\circ}$.
    The turn to $150^{\circ}$ means the interior angle at $B$ is $240^{\circ} - 150^{\circ} = 90^{\circ}$.

  Step 2: Use the cosine rule to find $AC$
    $$AC^2 = 12^2 + 16^2 - 2(12)(16)\cos 90^{\circ}$$
    $$AC^2 = 144 + 256 - 0 = 400$$
    $$AC = 20 	ext{ km}$$

  Step 3: Find the bearing of $C$ from $A$
    Use the sine rule to find the angle between $AB$ and $AC$:
    $$\dfrac{\sin \angle BAC}{16} = \dfrac{\sin 90^{\circ}}{20}$$
    $$\sin \angle BAC = \dfrac{16}{20} = 0.8$$
    $$\angle BAC \approx 53.1^{\circ}$$

    Bearing of $C$ from $A$ = $060^{\circ} + 53.1^{\circ} = 113.1^{\circ}$.

💡 Worked Example — Periodic Modelling
The depth of water in a harbour is modelled by $d(t) = 4 + 3\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\right)$ metres, where $t$ is hours after midnight. Find the first time after midnight when the depth is $6.5$ m.

  Step 1: Set up the equation
    $$4 + 3\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\right) = 6.5$$
    $$3\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\right) = 2.5$$
    $$\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\right) = \dfrac{5}{6}$$

  Step 2: Solve for $t$
    $$\dfrac{\pi t}{6} = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right) \approx 0.9851$$
    $$t \approx \dfrac{6 	imes 0.9851}{\pi} \approx 1.88 	ext{ hours}$$

    Converting $0.88$ hours to minutes: $0.88 	imes 60 \approx 53$ minutes.

  The first time is approximately 01:53.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• For trig equations, use identities to reduce to a single ratio.
• In 3D problems, identify right-angled triangles within the solid and use Pythagoras or trigonometry.
• Bearings are measured clockwise from north; always draw a clear diagram.
• Periodic models have the form $y = a\sin(b(t - c)) + d$; remember to account for amplitude, period, phase shift, and vertical shift.

⚠️ Common Mistake
When solving $\sin x = k$ over an interval, find all solutions by considering both quadrants where sine is positive (or negative) and adding multiples of the period. Do not stop at the principal value.

flashcards.definition: 1 rad = angle subtended by arc equal to radius. $2\pi$ rad = $360^{\circ}$.
$\sin 2	heta=2\sin	heta\cos	heta$; $\cos 2	heta=\cos^2	heta-\sin^2	heta$
$l = r	heta$ where $	heta$ is in radians.
$A = \dfrac{1}{2}r^2	heta$ where $	heta$ is in radians.
SSA with acute given angle and $a < b$ can give two triangles.
flashcards.example: $a=8, b=12, A=35^{\circ} \rightarrow$ two possible values for angle $B$.

flashcards.definition: Half the distance between the maximum and minimum values of a sinusoidal function; $|a|$ in $y = a\sin(b(x-c))+d$.
The length of one complete cycle. For $y=a\sin(b(x-c))+d$, period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{|b|}$.

questions.stem: $210^{\circ}$ in radians?
questions.explanation: $210 	imes \dfrac{\pi}{180} = \dfrac{7\pi}{6}$.

questions.stem: $\sin	heta=\dfrac{5}{13}$, $	heta$ in Q1. $\cos	heta$?
questions.explanation: $\sin^2	heta+\cos^2	heta=1$ \rightarrow $\cos^2	heta=\dfrac{144}{169}$ \rightarrow $\cos	heta=\dfrac{12}{13}$.

questions.stem: $y=4\sin(3x)-2$: amplitude and period?
questions.explanation: $|a|=4$, period $= \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

questions.stem: Solve $\sin	heta=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ for $0 \leq 	heta \leq 2\pi$.
questions.explanation: $\sin$ is positive in Q1, Q2 \rightarrow $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, $\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

questions.stem: $2\cos^2	heta-\cos	heta-1=0$ ($0^{\circ} \leq 	heta \leq 360^{\circ}$). Solutions?
questions.explanation: $u=\cos	heta$ \rightarrow $(2u+1)(u-1)=0$ \rightarrow $\cos	heta=1$ ($0^{\circ}$), $\cos	heta=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ ($120^{\circ},240^{\circ}$).

questions.stem: Triangle: $a=7,b=10,\angle A=35^{\circ}$. Area?
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{1}{2} 	imes 7 	imes 10 	imes \sin35^{\circ}$. Wait, $\sin35^{\circ}$ isn't exact. Let me fix: $\dfrac{1}{2} 	imes 7 	imes 10 	imes \sin60^{\circ} = 35 	imes \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. So the question should use $60^{\circ}$.

questions.stem: A lawn sprinkler rotates through $120^{\circ}$ and waters grass up to $5$ m from its centre. What area of lawn does it water?
questions.explanation: Convert $120^{\circ}$ to $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ rad. Sector area $A = \dfrac{1}{2}r^2	heta = \dfrac{1}{2} 	imes 25 	imes \dfrac{2\pi}{3} = \dfrac{25\pi}{3}$ m$^2$. $\dfrac{50\pi}{3}$ forgets the $\dfrac{1}{2}$ factor; $\dfrac{25\pi}{6}$ uses the wrong angle; $\dfrac{100\pi}{3}$ squares the radius incorrectly.

questions.stem: In $\Delta ABC$, $a = 8$, $b = 12$ and angle $A = 35^{\circ}$. How many distinct triangles can be formed?
questions.explanation: Using the sine rule: $\sin B = \dfrac{b \sin A}{a} \approx 0.860$. Since $a < b$ and angle $A$ is acute, and $\sin B < 1$, there are two possible values for angle $B$ (acute and obtuse), giving two valid triangles. This is the ambiguous case.

questions.stem: A triangle has sides $7$ cm, $10$ cm and $12$ cm. Find the largest angle.
questions.explanation: The largest angle is opposite the longest side ($12$ cm). Using the cosine rule: $\cos C = \dfrac{7^2 + 10^2 - 12^2}{2 	imes 7 	imes 10} = \dfrac{49 + 100 - 144}{140} = \dfrac{5}{140} = \dfrac{1}{28}$. So $C = \cos^{-1}(\dfrac{1}{28}) \approx 88.0^{\circ}$.

questions.stem: What is the period of $y = 3 \cos(2x - \dfrac{\pi}{4}) + 1$?
questions.explanation: For $y = a \cos(b(x - c)) + d$, the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{|b|}$. Here $b = 2$, so period $= \dfrac{2\pi}{2} = \pi$. $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ confuses the phase shift with the period; $2\pi$ ignores the horizontal compression; $4\pi$ incorrectly multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.stem: A ship sails $15$ km on bearing $070^{\circ}$, then turns to bearing $150^{\circ}$ and sails $20$ km. How far is it from its starting point?
questions.explanation: The angle between the two legs at the turn point is $100^{\circ}$ (back bearing $250^{\circ}$ minus new bearing $150^{\circ}$). Using the cosine rule: $d^2 = 15^2 + 20^2 - 2(15)(20)\cos(100^{\circ}) \approx 729$, so $d \approx 27.0$ km. $24.5$ km uses $80^{\circ}$ instead of $100^{\circ}$; $30.2$ km uses $60^{\circ}$; $35.0$ km simply adds the two distances.

questions.stem: A student claims: "If $\sin 	heta = 0.5$, then $	heta$ must be $30^{\circ}$." Which statement BEST explains why this is incorrect?
choices: Because $\sin 	heta$ is only positive in quadrant 1
Because $30^{\circ}$ is not the principal value
Because $\sin 	heta = 0.5$ also has solutions at $150^{\circ}$, $390^{\circ}$, and so on
Because calculators always give the wrong answer for inverse sine
questions.explanation: Sine is positive in both Q1 and Q2, so $	heta = 30^{\circ}$ and $	heta = 150^{\circ}$ both satisfy $\sin 	heta = 0.5$ in $[0^{\circ}, 360^{\circ}]$. Additionally, sine is periodic with period $360^{\circ}$, giving infinitely many solutions. Option A is false ($\sin$ is also positive in Q2). Option B is false ($30^{\circ}$ IS the principal value). Option D is nonsense.

questions.stem: Convert $\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ radians to degrees.
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{5\pi}{6} 	imes \dfrac{180^{\circ}}{\pi} = 150^{\circ}$.

questions.stem: Find the exact value of $\cos 15^{\circ}$.
questions.explanation: $\cos(45^{\circ}-30^{\circ}) = \cos45^{\circ}\cos30^{\circ} + \sin45^{\circ}\sin30^{\circ} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{6}+\sqrt{2}}{4}$.

questions.stem: What is the principal value of $	an^{-1}(-1)$?
questions.explanation: The principal range of $	an^{-1}$ is $(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2})$, and $	an(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}) = -1$.

questions.stem: Solve $3\sin^2 x - 5\cos x + 1 = 0$ for $0 \leq x \leq 2\pi$. How many solutions are there?
questions.explanation: Replace $\sin^2 x$ with $1 - \cos^2 x$ to get $3\cos^2 x + 5\cos x - 4 = 0$. This gives $\cos x = \dfrac{-5 + \sqrt{73}}{6} \approx 0.591$ (valid) or $\cos x = \dfrac{-5 - \sqrt{73}}{6} \approx -2.26$ (invalid). One valid cosine value yields two solutions in $[0, 2\pi]$.

questions.stem: A right pyramid has a square base of side $8$ cm and height $6$ cm. Find the angle between a sloping face and the base.
questions.explanation: The distance from the centre of the base to the midpoint of a side is $4$ cm. The slant height of a face is $\sqrt{4^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{52}$ cm. The angle $	heta$ between the face and the base satisfies $	an 	heta = \dfrac{6}{4} = 1.5$, so $	heta \approx 56.3^{\circ}$.

questions.stem: Two lighthouses P and Q are $25$ km apart on a north-south line, with P due north of Q. A ship S is on a bearing of $140^{\circ}$ from P and on a bearing of $060^{\circ}$ from Q. Find the distance QS.
questions.explanation: In triangle PQS, angle QPS = $180^{\circ} - 140^{\circ} = 40^{\circ}$ and angle PQS = $060^{\circ}$ (bearing from Q). Therefore angle PSQ = $80^{\circ}$. By the sine rule, $\dfrac{QS}{\sin 40^{\circ}} = \dfrac{25}{\sin 80^{\circ}}$, giving $QS \approx 16.3$ km.

questions.stem: The height of a seat on a Ferris wheel is modelled by $h(t) = 20 + 15\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{15}\right)$ metres, where $t$ is in minutes. For how many minutes in the first $30$ minutes is the seat more than $27.5$ m above the ground?
questions.explanation: Solve $20 + 15\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{15}\right) > 27.5$, which gives $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{15}\right) > 0.5$. In one period of $30$ minutes, this occurs between $t = 2.5$ and $t = 12.5$, a total of $10$ minutes.

questions.stem: Given $\sin 	heta - \cos 	heta = \dfrac{1}{3}$, find the value of $\sin 2	heta$.
questions.explanation: Square both sides: $(\sin 	heta - \cos 	heta)^2 = \dfrac{1}{9}$. This gives $\sin^2 	heta - 2\sin	heta\cos	heta + \cos^2	heta = \dfrac{1}{9}$, so $1 - \sin 2	heta = \dfrac{1}{9}$. Hence $\sin 2	heta = \dfrac{8}{9}$.
